title: Ashwin Was Named One of the 25 Greatest Cricketers of This Century. His Speech Was About Everyone Else.
excerpt: At the Cricinfo Honours Awards, the retired off-spinner asked the question Indian cricket doesn't want to answer: who will invest 20 years in first-class cricket when the IPL pays more in one season?
body:
Six months after walking away from international cricket, Ravichandran Ashwin received the kind of validation that makes retirement easier to accept — and harder for India to move on from.

At the Cricinfo Honours Awards 2026, Ashwin was named one of the 25 Greatest Men's International Cricketers of the 21st Century, a distinction that places him alongside the format-defining players of the modern era. He used the platform not for nostalgia, but to issue a challenge to the system that produced him.

## "How Do We Motivate Them?"

Ashwin's speech at the ceremony cut to the heart of Indian cricket's talent paradox. With 765 international wickets, five Test centuries, and a career that spanned 14 years across all formats, he could have taken a comfortable victory lap. Instead, he posed the question that keeps BCCI administrators up at night.

"How do we motivate these players to invest 15 to 20 years in first-class cricket amid lifestyle sacrifices and financial pressures?" Ashwin said. He was not speaking hypothetically. In a country where a single IPL season can earn a young cricketer more than a decade of Ranji Trophy appearances, the incentive structure for Test cricket has become inverted.

Ashwin's own path — from a middle-class Chennai household to the most prolific off-spinner in Indian Test history — was built on exactly the kind of sustained domestic investment he is now worried about losing. He took 537 Test wickets, the second-most for India behind Anil Kumble. He scored 3,503 Test runs, with a best of 124. He won 11 Player of the Series awards in Tests, the most by any player in history.

## The Numbers That Define a Generation

The scale of Ashwin's achievements becomes clearer in comparison. He is one of only three all-rounders in Test history to score 3,000 runs and take 500 wickets. He holds 100 or more international wickets against four different opponents — Australia (140), England (124), Sri Lanka (108), and West Indies (100) — matching Kapil Dev among Indians.

He was the fastest Indian to every milestone from 50 to 500 Test wickets by matches played. He was ICC Men's Cricketer of the Year in 2016. He received the Padma Shri in 2025, months after his final international appearance.

"Both batters and bowlers need to become problem-solvers, adjusting ball by ball," Ashwin said at the ceremony. It was a philosophy he embodied more than perhaps any cricketer of his era — constantly reinventing his variations, adding the carrom ball, the slider, the wide-of-crease angle that turned harmless tracks into minefields.

## What Test Cricket Looks Like Without Him

India are currently in the middle of a Test against Afghanistan in Mullanpur, their first since Ashwin's retirement. Manav Suthar, the left-arm spinner making his debut, has already taken three wickets. Washington Sundar scored a half-century. Kuldeep Yadav remains the primary spin threat.

But none of them possesses what Ashwin brought: the ability to think his way through a batting lineup, to set traps that unfolded over entire sessions, to bat at number eight and change the shape of a declaration. That combination may not exist again in Indian cricket for a generation.

## The Diaspora Legacy

For NRI cricket fans who grew up watching Ashwin dismantle England in Chennai and outfox Steve Smith in Dharamsala, the Cricinfo honour is a reminder of what Indian cricket looked like at its most cerebral. Ashwin represented a particular strain of Indian excellence — not the explosive six-hitting that fills social media feeds, but the patient, chess-like cricket that rewards watchers who understood every field placement.

His concern about the future of first-class cricket carries a particular resonance for the diaspora community. Many NRI parents who encourage their children to play cricket in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom do so because they believe the sport teaches discipline, strategy, and long-form thinking. If the domestic system that produced Ashwin withers under the weight of T20 economics, something irreplaceable will be lost — not just for India, but for the global game.

*Sources: Cricinfo Honours Awards 2026, Devdiscourse, ESPNcricinfo*
